saint.name: St. Pio of Pietrelcina
saint.summary: As a young priest in southern Italy, Saint Pio, known to the world as Padre Pio, begged God for one thing: to suffer, even to die of suffering, but all in hiding. Instead he lived fifty years with open wounds in his hands, his feet, and his side, and the world knew it. From 1918 he never left the Gargano mountain, so the sick, the curious, kings, and a young Polish priest climbed the hill to him. Rome restricted him and investigated him twice. He told one bishop, "In Holy Church it is God himself who speaks." He turned the crowds toward a confessional, an altar, and a hospital. The young Pole became Pope and declared him a saint.
saint.biography:
In the summer of 1923, the people of San Giovanni Rotondo heard that their friar’s superiors were going to take him away. The friary stood about a mile outside the town, on the slope of the Gargano mountain. The townspeople walked up to it together and would not leave until the friar showed himself at a window. After that forty local men took turns guarding the building, so that he could not be carried off in secret. That summer the Rome correspondent of the London Observer wrote about this friar. He did not describe a wonder-worker.

“Padre Pio himself lays no claim to miraculous gifts; he is the most modest and simple of men. He has a mild, ascetic countenance, with a fair beard, and hair turning grey on his high temples. His eyes are kind yet piercing; his voice has a peculiar charm.”

— The Observer, London, Rome correspondent, summer 1923

The man at the window was thirty-six years old. For five years he had carried open wounds in his hands, his feet, and his side, and much of Italy knew it. He had wanted no one to know. Years earlier he had written to his spiritual director about red marks in his palms and about “that cursed shame” that kept him silent. In his home village of Pietrelcina, people still tell how he begged the parish priest to pray with him. He wanted to suffer and even to die of suffering, but all in hiding.

In the end the wounds did not stay hidden. The friar was Saint Pio of Pietrelcina. The world still knows him as Padre Pio, which is Italian for Father Pio. Saint Pio carried them for fifty years and died without a scar. He stayed on that mountain for the rest of his life. The world came to him instead: the sick and the curious, doubters and sinners, kings and queens, and a young priest from Poland. The Church he obeyed tested him hard. It restricted him, silenced him, and investigated him twice. He answered every order with obedience, and he turned the crowds toward three things: the altar, the confessional, and a hospital on the mountain. Pope Saint Paul VI asked in 1971 why such a man had become famous. Saint Pio was not a philosopher or a scholar and had no means of his own, the Pope said. He said Mass humbly and heard confessions from morning to night. “He was a man of prayer and suffering.”

That man began as a shepherd boy in a hill village of the south.

Saint Pio Grows Up on a Farm

Saint Pio was born Francesco Forgione on 25 May 1887 in Pietrelcina, a hill village in the province of Benevento in southern Italy. His parents, Grazio and Maria Giuseppa, owned a few fields and worked them with their own hands. They were not poor by village standards. There was food every day and very little cash. Neither of them could read or write, but they knew the Bible stories by heart and told them to their children in the evenings. The baby was named after an older brother who had died in infancy.

Religion in that house was plain and practical. The dawn bell called them to prayer, and they went to Mass every day. At night they said the Rosary together. Three days a week they ate no meat, in honour of Our Lady of Mount Carmel. The neighbours had a name for them: the God-is-everything people. The family land lay at Piana Romana, outside the village, with grapes and wheat, olives and figs, and a few animals. Saint Pio minded the sheep there until he was about ten. He went to school when the farm work allowed. He had typhoid at ten and recovered.

Something else began early. He said many years later that as a boy of five he saw Our Lady and the Sacred Heart of Jesus in the village church. He thought every child saw them. The boy sang hymns and played at saying Mass. One of his biographers tells that at five he gave himself to Jesus for good.

Then a friar came through. A young Capuchin called Fra Camillo walked the countryside around Pietrelcina, begging for his friary at Morcone. He wore a brown robe and a beard, and the boy was drawn to him. Saint Pio told his parents that he wanted to be a friar like that one, a friar with a beard. He said later that the beard stayed so fixed in his mind that nothing could turn him from the wish.

His parents took him seriously. They went thirteen miles north to Morcone and asked whether the Capuchins would take their son. The friars were interested, but the boy had three years of village school and would need much more before they could accept him. A private tutor cost money, and the small farm did not earn enough. So Grazio Forgione did what thousands of men from the south were doing in those years. He went to America to find work. Saint Pio studied with a village priest, and when the friars at Morcone first said no to his papers, the family waited and asked again. In the autumn of 1902 the answer was yes.

He left home in January 1903, at fifteen, and travelled to Morcone by oxcart. On 22 January he put on the brown robe and received the name Pio. The name came from Saint Pius V, the patron saint of Pietrelcina. The boy who had wanted a beard now had the robe to go with it. What he did not have was a body that could stand the life.

Saint Pio Joins the Capuchins and Falls Ill

The Capuchins are a branch of the Franciscans, the brothers of Saint Francis of Assisi. They keep a hard rule: fasting, long prayers at night, bare cells, and work in the poorest places. Saint Pio took his first vows in 1904 and then moved from friary to friary for his studies, as young friars did. Within two years he was ill. He could not keep food down, he fainted, and his head ached. For a time he could digest only milk and cheese. The illness came and went for the rest of his youth.

In the school year of 1907 to 1908 he studied theology at the friary of Serracapriola. His teacher there was Padre Agostino da San Marco in Lamis, a friar who would guide him for many years. Padre Agostino wrote of the student in his diary. “He was good, obedient, studious, though sickly.” Part of the sickness came from his prayer. Saint Pio meditated on the Passion of Christ, and he wept over it so much that his eyes became sick. On Good Friday 1908 he already had trouble in his chest, and a migraine took hold of him and lasted the rest of his stay. He missed lessons, and he had almost no appetite. That summer he wrote to his parents that the heat made it a little hard to be there, and he told them not to worry.

The friars worried instead. His pains seemed to have no end and his appetite stayed poor, so they sent a telegram to the parish priest of Pietrelcina. The priest sent for Grazio Forgione. The father came to Serracapriola, slept in the friary, and listened to the doctor who had examined his son. Then he took the boy home for a rest.

This became the pattern of the next years. Saint Pio would go back to a friary, fall ill, and be sent to a house in the mountains or back home. In early 1909 he was living in Pietrelcina again. Through all of it he kept studying, and his superiors kept him moving toward the priesthood. The Church then required a priest to be twenty-four. On 10 August 1910 the archbishop of Benevento made an exception for a sick young friar of twenty-three and ordained him in the chapel of his cathedral. Four days later Saint Pio said his first Mass in the church of Our Lady of the Angels in Pietrelcina.

He did not go back to a friary. His superiors sent him home on health leave. There he kept the robe, said Mass each morning, and taught a few children. The leave lasted six years with short breaks. Saint Pio was a priest at twenty-three and too sick to live with his brothers. In one letter of these years he described what Holy Communion had become to him. Before he received Christ he felt such hunger and thirst that he nearly died of longing. Sometimes he went to the altar with a fever on him, because he could not stay away. The illness had not touched the one thing he lived for. Within weeks of his first Mass, something would happen to his hands.

Saint Pio Hides His First Wounds

Every morning after Mass, Saint Pio walked out of the village to the family land at Piana Romana. His brother Michele had built him a hut there, and he prayed in the open air under an elm tree. The air helped his lungs. On the afternoon of 7 September 1910 something happened under that elm. It was a month after his ordination. He kept silent about it for almost a year.

On 8 September 1911 he wrote to his spiritual director, Padre Benedetto, and said what it was. A little red mark the size of a cent coin had appeared in the middle of each palm. It came with a strong and sharp pain that was worse in the left hand. There was some pain under his feet too. The marks had been there for almost a year, and he had kept silent about them because of “that cursed shame”.

The first person in the village to know was the parish priest, Don Salvatore Pannullo. Everyone called him Zi’ Tore, Uncle Tore. The two men prayed together over it, and the story of what Saint Pio said to him is still told in Pietrelcina.

“Zi’ Tore, do me the kindness: let us ask Jesus to take this shame from me. I want to suffer, even to die of suffering, but all in hiding.”

— Saint Pio to Don Salvatore Pannullo, as told in Pietrelcina

The old priest said he would help him pray. But he told Saint Pio that if this was God’s will, he must bend to it, as to God’s will in all things. Four years later Padre Agostino sent him three written questions and asked him in the name of Jesus to answer them. When had the visions begun? Did he have the stigmata? Did he feel the crown of thorns and the scourging? Saint Pio first avoided the questions, then answered. The visions had begun in his first year as a friar. The marks had been visible, “especially in one hand”. He had prayed and they had been taken away. The very sharp pain had not gone, and he felt it most on certain days. He felt the thorns and the scourging most weeks.

In the autumn of 1911 he went to the friary of Venafro to recover, and he stayed about forty days. The friars there saw things they had never seen. Padre Agostino and the superior of the house watched him fall into states of prayer. In them he spoke aloud with Jesus, with Mary, with Saint Francis, and with his guardian angel, the way a man talks with people in the room. Padre Agostino began to write down what he heard. His first notebook opens with what he heard at Venafro on 28 November 1911, from a quarter to ten until eleven in the morning. In it Saint Pio says to Jesus, “It is so sweet to be with you! Oh, how good it is here!” He asks to be allowed to feed on him every morning. The EWTN biography tells how Padre Agostino heard that the young priest was ill, ran in, and found a man who seemed to be dying. He went to the chapel to pray, and came back to find him alert and full of joy. Padre Agostino also saw the devil attack him. On 7 December Saint Pio went home.

For the next four years Saint Pio lived in Pietrelcina, mostly in his brother Michele’s house, and wrote to his two directors under obedience. They now fill the first volume of his collected letters, and they let us see his life with God from the inside. In November 1913 he described what happened when he prayed. As soon as he began to pray, his soul gathered into a peace and quiet that no words could express. His senses were held still, all but his hearing. Great noise around him did not disturb him. The same letters show the dark side. In May 1913 he wrote that he had dared to ask Our Lady again for a grace she had refused him. “This Holy Mother flew into a rage,” he wrote, and she withdrew from him with the other heavenly persons. In another time of dryness he wrote simply: “I seek God, but where can I find him?” The wish to suffer runs through them. “I want to suffer,” one letter says. “This is my longing.”

The letters have one more mark of the man. Saint Pio ended them again and again with the same request: pray hard for my conversion. In November 1915 a different letter arrived. Italy had been at war for six months, and the army was calling up the priest with the bad lungs.

Saint Pio Leaves the Army and Teaches Boys

The army put him in the medical corps in Naples in December 1915. At the first medical exam the army doctors found trouble in his lungs and sent him home on a year’s leave. That became the pattern of his war: a call-up, then a hospital bed and another leave. He did not serve at the front. In between he lived at a friary in Foggia, on the hot plain of Puglia. There he sweated and ran fevers through the spring of 1916. In late July Padre Paolino da Casacalenda took him up to San Giovanni Rotondo for a few days. The air was cooler there and he felt better at once. He wrote to his superiors and asked to stay, because Jesus had assured him he would be well there. On 4 September 1916 he was sent to the friary of Santa Maria delle Grazie “provisionally”. He stayed for fifty-two years.

The friary was small and poor. A handful of friars lived in it about a mile above the town. Beside it stood a little church and a boarding school for boys who hoped to become friars. A week after he arrived Saint Pio wrote to Padre Agostino that he had found a most devout community and that his “night of the spirit” was growing. Padre Paolino slipped his own note into the envelope. It said that Saint Pio could be called really happy, apart from the inner pains with which the Lord wished to test him.

The army soon began to empty the house. In February 1917 the director of the boys’ school was called up, and in December another priest followed. That left two priests for the whole friary: Padre Paolino and Saint Pio. The sick friar became the guide of the boys. He heard their confessions and gave them two talks a week. He watched over their study and their weekly walk, joined their games, led them at table, and prayed with them. The people of the town had begun to climb the hill as well. In July 1917 he wrote to Padre Agostino that he had no time even to rest in the heart of the Father. Caring for the boys and helping souls by word and by letter took all of it. Then he wrote a line that fit the rest of his life: “I do not know how to say no to anyone.”

In January 1917 pneumonia and typhoid put him to bed. Padre Paolino took his temperature. He was the guardian, the superior of the friary. Afterward he said that the ordinary thermometer burst and that a bath thermometer read fifty-two degrees Celsius. In the summer of 1917 the army took Saint Pio back to the military hospital in Naples for three months. In March 1918 it finally discharged him for a disease of both lungs. He came home to the friary on 17 March.

That spring Pope Benedict XV asked priests to offer themselves for the end of the war. Saint Pio made that offering at Mass on 30 May 1918, the feast of Corpus Christi. He wrote afterward that he fell into a lasting state he could only call imprisonment in hell. Meanwhile Padre Paolino was seeing things in his friend that he had not seen before. Twice between March and September he found him in ecstasy and heard him speaking with Jesus and Mary. He saw for himself that Saint Pio could read what was in a person’s heart.

On the evening of 5 August 1918 Saint Pio was hearing the boys’ confessions. He wrote to Padre Benedetto that all at once he was filled with terror at the sight of a heavenly figure. The figure held something like a very long blade of iron with a sharp point, and fire seemed to come from the point. He barely let out a cry. “I felt I was dying,” he wrote. The pain lasted until the morning of 7 August, and when it passed it left something behind. In the depth of his soul he felt “a wound that is always open”. He was tired, he added, and only obedience to his director kept him from giving up completely.

Padre Benedetto wrote back that 6 August was the feast of the Transfiguration, and that the wound was a sign of God’s love. Six weeks later the sign became visible.

Saint Pio Receives the Wounds of Christ

On the morning of Friday 20 September 1918 the friary was nearly empty. Padre Paolino was away at San Marco in Lamis. The brother who begged for the friary was out on his rounds. Saint Pio said Mass in the little church. Then he went up to give thanks in the choir, the friars’ prayer loft above the church door. It was between nine and ten o’clock, and by his own account no one else was there.

He told no one what happened next: not his superior, not Padre Benedetto, and not even Padre Agostino. A month later Padre Benedetto ordered him under obedience to write it all down, and on 22 October he did. The letter begins with a cry: “My God, what confusion and humiliation I feel.” Then it tells the story in a few lines. After Mass in the choir he was overcome by “a rest, like a sweet sleep”. All his senses went still. Before him stood a mysterious figure like the one of 5 August, and this time its hands and feet and side were dripping blood. The sight terrified him. “I felt I was dying,” he wrote, and he would have died if the Lord had not held up his heart. The figure withdrew. When Saint Pio looked down, his own hands, feet, and side were pierced and bleeding.

The letter says nothing about how he left the choir. An account handed down by word of mouth comes from Saint Pio’s talk with his friend Don Peppino Orlando. In that account a great light struck his eyes. Christ appeared, said nothing, and vanished. He came to on the floor. On all fours he dragged himself from the choir to his cell. There he lay on his bed, prayed, looked at the wounds, and wept.

He meant to keep the wounds a secret. But the friary had only two priests, and the town climbed the hill to see him. The secret lasted a day. A woman named Filomena Ventrella saw red marks on his hands on the 20th. Her sister remembered that he warned them to tell no one. On the Saturday morning the boys of the school noticed a wound in each of his palms. He walked with difficulty, and his face was redder than usual.

That afternoon Nina Campanile came up from the town. She kept a diary, and she had kissed his hand on the 18th and seen nothing. He teased her that she had stayed away for three days while he waited for a Mary to bring him a word of comfort. She handed him a Mass offering and saw something in the middle of the back of his right hand. It looked like a burn. She decided to act as if she did not understand what she was seeing, and she cried out: “Oh, Father! You have burned your hand!” Saint Pio turned pale and put both hands behind his back.

When she left she tried to kiss the wound. “If you knew what humiliation you give me!” he said. He told her he would pray so hard that the Lord would make all of it disappear. And he meant it. He had prayed once before, and the marks had been taken away.

Nina kept the secret for eight or ten days. Then she told Padre Paolino with a smile, and he laughed out loud. Was it possible that Saint Pio had received the stigmata and that the guardian who was with him all day had not noticed? The next day he went to Saint Pio’s cell and walked in without knocking. Saint Pio was writing. The guardian saw the wounds on the back and the palm of the right hand, then the wound on the back of the left. He wrote to Padre Benedetto the same day and asked him to come. Padre Benedetto did not come. He asked instead that everyone keep the strictest silence.

Saint Pio’s own letters from that autumn show what the silence cost. On 17 October he asked whether he must say his yes to God as he looked at “that mysterious figure who has wounded me all over”. In the great letter of 22 October he wrote of a constant roar inside him, like a waterfall that always pours out blood. He ended with a prayer. He said that the punishment was just and God’s judgment right, and at the end he begged for mercy. Later in the year he told Padre Benedetto that the wound in his side bled from Thursday evening to Saturday. The pain was killing him, and so was the shame that came after it. “I fear I will bleed to death.” And yet a later letter speaks to the pain itself as if to a friend. He calls his torments sweet and bitter together, wounding and healing at once. He asks why they can be so unbearable and so dear.

Padre Benedetto came at last at the start of Lent 1919. He saw the friar barely able to stand at the altar, and on Ash Wednesday he wrote to Padre Agostino what he had seen. He called the marks “true wounds” that pierced the hands and the feet. On Fridays they bled. When Saint Pio said Mass he had to hold his hands raised and bare, so everyone could see the gift.

Padre Benedetto let him go on saying Mass, so anyone in the church could see the wounds. In May 1919 the newspapers of Rome began to print stories about a friar in the Gargano with the wounds of Christ. The doctors came next.

Doctors and a Bishop Examine Saint Pio

The Capuchins themselves sent the first doctor. Dr Luigi Romanelli was head surgeon of the hospital at Barletta, and he examined Saint Pio on 15 and 16 May 1919 by order of the provincial superior. His report is careful and plain. The wounds on the hands were covered by a reddish-brown membrane. There was no bleeding point, no swelling, and no inflammation in the skin around them. He was sure the wounds were not shallow. When he pressed his thumb into the palm and his finger on the back of the hand, he could feel the empty space between them. He came back four more times over the next year and did not change his mind.

In July a Roman professor of pathology named Amico Bignami came to look. He saw the same wounds and described them the same way, but he judged them differently. In his view they had begun as a disease of the skin. He thought that suggestion or a chemical such as tincture of iodine had completed them, perhaps without the friar knowing it. In the autumn a third doctor named Giorgio Festa came, and he went on coming for years. He measured the fevers that went with the wounds and said some of them ran higher than a clinical thermometer could register. In 1925 he sent a report to the Holy Office. This was the Vatican department that watched over faith and morals. He wrote that the wounds were not the work of any outside injury or strong chemical.

In April 1920 a famous visitor came to the friary: Padre Agostino Gemelli, a Franciscan friar and a well-known doctor. He asked to examine the wounds. Saint Pio asked to see his written authorization from the Holy Office. Gemelli had none, and the superiors of the friary took Saint Pio’s side. Gemelli left offended, without having seen the wounds at all. He wrote a hard letter all the same. He called the whole thing a bluff and the friar a hysteric.

Saint Pio hid what he could. He wore red mittens or black coverings over his hands and feet, and said he was embarrassed. At Mass the mittens had to come off. Visitors began to arrive from far away, and the first foreign newspapers took notice. In November 1920 a Catholic weekly in Australia, the Southern Cross, told its readers what little it knew.

“That there is a priest in Southern Italy marked with the stigmata is scarcely known at the moment.”

— The Southern Cross, Australia, November 1920

The paper added that the wounds gave him more pain than usual every Friday. Doctors had examined them without reaching any opinion. The one thing they agreed on was that the wounds could not be explained from a natural standpoint.

Rome wanted its own opinion. In June 1921 the Holy Office sent a bishop to San Giovanni Rotondo in secret. Bishop Raffaello Carlo Rossi of Volterra arrived on 14 June and stayed eight days. His inquiry recorded 142 detailed answers. He asked about the wounds and about the stories that Saint Pio had been seen in two places at once. Then he asked the question the Holy Office cared about most. Would he always submit to the authority of the Church?

“Yes, Excellency. In Holy Church it is God himself who speaks.”

— Saint Pio to Bishop Raffaello Carlo Rossi, June 1921

The bishop wanted to stay cool and fair, and he wrote that he felt almost cold toward the whole affair. Even so, he wrote down what he found. Everyone at the friary spoke of a scent like violets around the friar, and Bishop Rossi smelled it himself. “I have smelled it,” he wrote, “just as I have seen the stigmata.” He finished his report on 4 October 1921. He wrote that Saint Pio was a good friar and a model, practised in the virtues. The bishop also wrote that Saint Pio shone with a heartfelt humility and a singular simplicity. He could not confirm many of the healings people told him about. Some of Saint Pio’s letters gave credible accounts, but without a doctor’s word he left the question open. About the stigmata he was sure. In his report they were a real fact, and he found neither fraud nor the devil’s work.

The report went to Rome. The Holy Office did not follow it. In June 1922 it imposed its first restrictions on Saint Pio. In May 1923 it issued a decree, and the Vatican newspaper printed it in July. The decree said that the Church could not establish that anything supernatural had taken place in Saint Pio. His town had a great deal to say about that.

Rome Restricts Saint Pio, and His Town Protests

The orders arrived in June 1923. Saint Pio was to say Mass only in the friary’s private chapel, with no one present, and he was to stop answering letters. The people of San Giovanni Rotondo found out within days. On 26 June they protested in such numbers that the friars let him say Mass in the church again. Rome then tried a different answer. On 30 July the head of all the Capuchins signed an order moving Saint Pio to a friary in the Marche, far to the north on the Adriatic coast.

Padre Luigi Festa was the friar sent to carry out the order. He read it to Saint Pio at midnight on 8 August, in the friary. Saint Pio stood with his arms folded and bowed his head. He said he was at Padre Luigi’s service and would leave at once. “When I am with my superior,” he said, “I am with God.”

He asked only one thing: to be sent to Montefusco, inside his own province, instead of out of it. Padre Luigi answered that nothing would happen until Rome sent further word. The order was never carried out. Two days later a mason from the town named Donato Centra walked into the church with a pistol. He said that Saint Pio would stay with them, alive or dead. On the evening of 15 August eight men of the local Fascist party climbed the hill with clubs to ask him to stay. The mayor Francesco Morcaldi arranged with the head of the Fascist militia to have the friary watched day and night. The prefect of the province said that the order could be carried out even if people died. This was the summer when the town marched up the hill and would not go home until Saint Pio came to a window. It was the summer when forty men took turns on guard at the door.

Saint Pio was very worried. On 12 August he wrote to the mayor. He was upset at the thought that he might cause deaths without wanting to, and he asked the mayor to help him carry out the will of his superiors. Then he asked for one thing in return. When he died, he wanted his bones to rest in a quiet corner of that land. On 21 August the head of the order told the mayor that the move was put off for now. On 27 August Saint Pio wrote again, this time to Padre Luigi. He would obey any order he was given. But without special help from God his leaving would mean dead priests, damaged churches, and danger to his own life. At the end of August a senior government official said that the move could not be made without bloodshed. In early September the order was quietly set aside. Saint Pio never left San Giovanni Rotondo again.

Rome did not lift the restrictions. Through the 1920s he said Mass and heard confessions under a cloud. His mother came to spend Christmas of 1928 near the friary, in the house of a spiritual daughter named Mary Pyle. His mother caught pneumonia there and died in the first days of January 1929. In the spring of 1931 a harder blow fell. The Holy See forbade him every priestly act except Mass said in private. No confessions, no public Mass, and no people. He obeyed for two years. The Church’s own record of his life says that he bore in silence both his superiors’ measures and the slanders behind them.

The silence ended as suddenly as it had begun. On 16 July 1933 Pope Pius XI allowed him to say Mass in public again. His biographers say that the Pope told an archbishop he had never been badly disposed toward Saint Pio, only badly informed. In March 1934 men were allowed to confess to him, and in May the women. In 1939 the new Pope Pius XII went further and encouraged people to visit him. The crowds came back up the mountain. Saint Pio had a plan for them.

Saint Pio Builds a Hospital on the Mountain

The idea was not new. In 1925 an old convent in the town had been turned into a small clinic with a few beds for the worst cases. An earthquake destroyed it in 1938. At the end of 1939 Saint Pio spoke to one of his spiritual sons, a veterinarian from Perugia named Mario Sanvico. He told him he wanted a hospital close to the friary. A real one.

On the evening of 9 January 1940 a small group met in a cottage near the friary. The Sanvico family lived there with the family of a doctor named Guglielmo Sanguinetti. Dr Sanvico was there with his wife. Dr Sanguinetti and his wife were there too, with a pharmacist and his wife and one other woman. All of them had put their souls in Saint Pio’s hands, and now they formed a committee. The paper they signed said that nothing would be done without first asking the advice of Saint Pio. Then they went to the friary and told him. He approved, and then he gave them a small coin that a Swiss visitor had given him that morning. “I also want to give my offering.” The others gave small sums of their own. He said that night that his earthly work had begun.

Two days later he pointed out the place where the hospital would stand. On 14 January he gave it a name: Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza, the Home for the Relief of Suffering. Then Italy went to war, in June 1940, and everything stopped for six years.

Work began again in 1946, and the first stone was laid on 16 May 1947. The work began without an architect’s plan, with four million lire in the bank. Money came in ways no one expected. A British relief worker named Barbara Ward heard Saint Pio’s Mass and met one of his doctors. She asked that part of the United Nations fund for rebuilding Italy go to the Home. The fund gave 325,000 dollars. A poor widow gave a fifty-lira note, and Saint Pio kept it in the pocket of his robe and took it out to show people, sometimes in tears. A layman named Gino Ghisleri searched Italy for doctors, nurses, and a community of nursing sisters willing to come to a mountain town in the south. When the sisters came from Milan, one of them said she prayed with Saint Pio every morning at the hour of his Mass.

The Home for the Relief of Suffering opened on 5 May 1956. One witness remembered a bright, sunny day. The building had some 250 beds and two operating theatres. There were departments of medicine, heart disease, bones, children, and childbirth. It had an X-ray unit, a laboratory, and a blood bank. It even had its own farm for milk, eggs, poultry, and oil. Cardinal Lercaro opened it in the Pope’s name. An international conference of heart specialists ran alongside the opening. One of them was the American heart doctor Paul Dudley White. He pressed close to Saint Pio with a camera and congratulated him on his wounds. Saint Pio spoke a few words to the crowd. He said that a seed had been sown on the earth and that God would warm it with the rays of his love. This would be a place of prayer and science. When people praised him for the building he answered that the Work belonged to Providence, not to him. He added that he would have built it of gold if he could.

Now a friar with a vow of poverty was in charge of a great deal of money. In 1957 Pius XII released him from the vow so that he could oversee the project. His enemies later said the money had been misused. Saint Pio himself spoke of the hospital in terms of prayer. He said that without prayer the Home for the Relief of Suffering was like a plant without air and sun. The sick came, and so did everyone else. By 1950 so many people wanted to confess to him that the friary had to set up a booking system.

Crowds Line Up at Saint Pio’s Confessional

A summer morning at San Giovanni Rotondo in the 1950s began in the dark. Saint Pio rose long before four to prepare for Mass. Women were already queuing for the old church. Some came at two or three in the morning to get the best places. Others came late and pushed to the front anyway. Once some of them chained a stool to the altar rail the night before, so that no one could take the seat. On her first visit a woman named Mrs Ghisleri took her place at the church door at half past two and was knocked down and trampled.

The Mass began at about five at the side altar of Saint Francis. It was in Latin, and it lasted about an hour and a half. A Scottish writer named John McCaffery served it seven times. The church was crowded. When it ended the men followed Saint Pio into the sacristy and stood without a word while he took off his vestments and prayed with his head bowed. Years before, he had written to one of his spiritual daughters about what the Mass meant to him. He told her that the world could do without the sun but not without the Holy Mass.

Those who knew him remembered other sayings. He used to say that in the Mass there is all of Calvary. He called it a tremendous ministry. Pope Saint John Paul II later put it in one line: the altar and the confessional were the two poles of his life.

The rest of the day belonged to the second pole. For fifty years Saint Pio sat in the confessional hour after hour, in the summer heat and the winter cold. Women confessed in the open confessional in the church. Men confessed in a screened box in the sacristy. Pilgrims put their names on a numbered list and waited for days until their turn came. He was not an easy confessor. He could seem severe. Pope Saint John Paul II had gone to him for confession as a young man. The Pope said later that pilgrims met with apparent severity, and that almost all of them came back. In 1994 he named Saint Pio and Saint John Vianney, the Curé of Ars, as two of the great confessors of the Church.

McCaffery collected the stories. One was about a Communist from Tuscany named Giovanni who drove to San Giovanni Rotondo in his taxi. In the confessional he wept, and he pulled out his party card and asked Saint Pio to destroy it. McCaffery also collected the jokes, and he said afterward that his memories of Saint Pio were soaked in humour more than in anything else. To a husband with a talkative wife, Saint Pio offered to take fifty per cent of her and leave him the rest. McCaffery once told him that his own old college rector was waiting in the corridor. Saint Pio raised his eyes to heaven in mock horror and begged God to save us from all such. Another day McCaffery told him that a Jesuit superior had wondered aloud how his humility survived the crowds. Saint Pio laughed hard. He said he would have to be mad or a thief to keep for himself what belonged to God. He wrote short notes on prayer cards for visitors and laughed at his own scrawls. As for the scent of violets that followed him, he said it was just sweets for the children.

Saint Pio did all this on one meal a day, which he ate under obedience: a spoonful of soup or a forkful of pasta, rice, or vegetables. The wounds stayed open. One day as the hot weather came on McCaffery asked him how he was. He answered in a weary voice. “It is the nights.” If he let himself sleep, the pain in the wounds was multiplied beyond measure. Bishop Rossi had written of his singular simplicity in 1921. The jokes and the nights belonged to the same man.

The crowds kept growing. Allied soldiers came up the mountain after 1943, and articles by American soldiers in Catholic papers brought Americans after the war. A new and larger church was consecrated beside the old one on 1 July 1959. Saint Pio was ill in hospital that day and missed it. The faithful kept coming, and so did the accusations. In 1960 Rome decided to look at him again.

Rome Investigates Saint Pio a Second Time

The new Pope was Saint John XXIII, and the reports that reached him in 1960 were ugly. Some said that Saint Pio had improper relations with the women who surrounded him. Some said that the hospital’s money was being misused, and that fanatics had gathered around the friar. There was also something new. Someone had hidden listening devices at San Giovanni Rotondo. In the early summer of 1960 an official of the Holy Office named Pietro Parente told the Pope about the recordings. One biographer says the tapes held nothing but humming and the soft voices of the confessional.

On 25 June 1960 the Pope wrote four sheets of private notes. They stayed unpublished for nearly fifty years. He wrote of the charges against the friar with a careful condition: “if what is reported is true”. He wrote about himself too. By the Lord’s grace he felt calm and almost unmoved. Then he wrote about Saint Pio.

“I am sorry for Padre Pio. He still has a soul to save, and I pray hard for him.”

— Pope Saint John XXIII, private notes, 25 June 1960

The Pope sent a visitor to San Giovanni Rotondo, Monsignor Carlo Maccari. His orders were to look into the whole affair and to curb the forms of popular devotion that Rome now found backward. Maccari held nine meetings with Saint Pio. In his diary he judged the friar harshly. He wrote of reticence, narrowness of mind, and lies, and he summed up his impression in one word: pitiful. He saw too much mixing of the sacred with the all-too-human, and he feared the fanatics around the friar. Maccari sent his recommendations to Rome. The friars should be moved out gradually, and a superior from outside should be brought in. Each penitent should be allowed one confession a month, and the hospital should have new statutes.

No one wrote down what Saint Pio said about the microphones or the nine meetings. The biographer Renzo Allegri records a saying of his: the Church is a mother even when she punishes. Padre Rosario da Aliminusa was the guardian of the friary at the time. He wrote that Saint Pio never failed in obedience.

A Capuchin writer later told how the story of the tapes ended. The archbishop of Manfredonia went to the Pope and explained that the kisses on the recordings were his own sister kissing the friar’s hand. The Pope lifted his eyes and said, “God be praised!” Even so, the restrictions stayed in place for four more years. Saint Pio was past seventy, and he sat in the confessional under a cloud for the second time in his life.

Then a letter came from Poland.

A Polish Bishop Asks Saint Pio for Help

Saint John Paul II was born Karol Wojtyła. He had visited San Giovanni Rotondo once before, as a young Polish priest studying in Rome just after the war. He stayed nearly a week and went to Saint Pio’s Mass and confessed to him. During the Mass he noticed the black scabs that covered the wounds on the friar’s hands. Years later he wrote to the guardian of the friary about that visit. He said that he had spoken with Saint Pio in person and exchanged a few words. He counted that first meeting the most important.

By November 1962 Saint John Paul II was a bishop and was in Rome for the Second Vatican Council. Back in Kraków a friend of his was gravely ill. Wanda Półtawska was a doctor and the mother of four daughters, and she had survived a German concentration camp in the war. Now she had cancer, and the surgeons had set a date to operate. On 17 November he wrote a short letter to Saint Pio in Latin.

“Venerable Father, I ask you to pray for a mother of four girls in Kraków, Poland. In the last war she spent five years in a German concentration camp. Now her health and her life are in great danger from cancer. May God show his mercy to her and her family, through the Blessed Virgin.”

— Saint John Paul II, then a bishop in Kraków, to Saint Pio, 17 November 1962

Angelo Battisti was an official of the Secretariat of State who also ran the Home for the Relief of Suffering. A cardinal in Rome handed him the letter and told him to take it to Saint Pio at once. Battisti drove south. The letter looked to him like one more request among many. He found Saint Pio in his cell at prayer. Saint Pio told him to open the letter and read it. Battisti read the Latin aloud, and Saint Pio listened without a word. Battisti said later that Saint Pio then raised his head. “Angelo, to this one it is not possible to say no!” Then he bowed his head again and went back to his prayer.

A few days later the doctors in Kraków prepared to operate. When they examined Wanda Półtawska before the surgery, they found nothing to operate on. Eleven days after his first letter Saint John Paul II wrote to Saint Pio again. He thanked him and said that the woman had been suddenly cured before the operation. Battisti said that Saint Pio later told him to keep the letters. “Little Angelo, save these letters, because one day they will become important.” Battisti kept them. On 16 October 1978 Saint John Paul II was elected Pope, and Battisti said he remembered those words.

The cloud over the friary lifted at last on 30 July 1964. Pope Saint Paul VI restored Saint Pio’s full freedom to say Mass and hear confessions as he pleased. He also placed the friar’s financial affairs under the Holy See. The Church changed the Mass the next year. The same Pope allowed the old friar to keep saying it in Latin as he always had, and later to say it sitting down. Meanwhile the crowds had not gone away. In September 1968 the prayer groups Saint Pio had founded sent delegates to the friary from seven countries, from Switzerland and England to India and Brazil. They came to mark fifty years since the wounds.

The Death of Saint Pio

The anniversary Mass was moved to Sunday, 22 September 1968, and sung as a solemn Mass because of the crowds. Television crews were in the church. Saint Pio was eighty-one and so weak that he nearly fell on the altar steps, and the friars held him up. At one point in the Mass he was confused. At the end he fainted and was carried to his room, and when he came down again to bless the people he fainted a second time. Moved, a friar wished him well on the fiftieth anniversary. Saint Pio answered almost absent-mindedly. “Fifty-eight,” he said. Counted from the elm tree in 1910, it was fifty-eight.

For three years a young friar named Padre Pellegrino Funicelli had slept in a room linked to Saint Pio’s by an intercom. The old man could call him in the night. That Sunday evening Saint Pio was in bed by nine. Between nine and midnight he called Padre Pellegrino five or six times to ask what time it was. He seemed quieter than usual and given to prayer, and his eyes were wet. On the wall hung a portrait of his mother. He said that he could see two mothers there.

At midnight he asked Padre Pellegrino to stay with him, and he held the younger man’s hand tightly. He was trembling like a child with a fever. At about one o’clock he asked whether Mass had been said yet. Padre Pellegrino told him it was too early. Saint Pio said that Padre Pellegrino would say it for him that morning. Then he asked to make his confession. After it he asked Padre Pellegrino to help him renew his religious vows.

There was one more request. He asked Padre Pellegrino to beg his brothers’ forgiveness for all the trouble he had caused them, and to ask them to pray for his soul. Then he blessed his brothers, his spiritual children, and the sick. He sent his love to his niece Pia, to his nephew, and to Sister Pia. He said they knew how much he had loved them.

Soon after one he said that he could not breathe lying down. He got up, washed his face, and combed his hair. Then he walked out to the verandah straight and unaided, fast, like a young man. The two friars sat and looked at the stars for about ten minutes. Then Saint Pio grew pale. Padre Pellegrino got him into a wheelchair and back inside, and then into an armchair. His lips were turning blue. He was repeating two names, over and over and more and more faintly: “Jesus, Mary. Jesus, Mary.” Padre Pellegrino moved to get help. “No!” Saint Pio said. “Do not disturb anybody.”

Padre Pellegrino went anyway. He ran for another friar and for the doctor, and two doctors on night duty at the hospital came up the hill. They gave oxygen and injections, and a priest anointed him. At about half past two in the morning of 23 September 1968 Saint Pio bowed his head gently toward his shoulder and went to God. One of the doctors said it was the most serene death he had ever seen.

When the friars prepared the body, they looked for the wounds. There were none. The doctor who had been at the bedside found the hands, the feet, and the side completely healed, without trace or scar. The wounds had faded in the last days before his death. By his own account he had carried them since the afternoon under the elm tree in 1910, and in public since 20 September 1918. The photographs of the body show no sign of them. His brothers laid him out in the church in his robe, and the pilgrims filed past until the funeral.

The funeral was held on 26 September. More than a hundred thousand people came from all over Italy, and the coffin was carried in procession through the town. That evening the friars buried him in the crypt beneath the church of Our Lady of Grace, in a quiet corner of the land he had asked for in 1923.

How Saint Pio’s Hospital and Prayer Groups Grew

Two and a half years after the funeral, Pope Saint Paul VI met the superiors of the Capuchin order and talked about the friar his predecessors had investigated. The Pope asked them to look at the fame Saint Pio had and at the people who gathered round him from all over the world. Why? Was he a philosopher? A scholar? Did he have means at his disposal? No. He said Mass humbly and heard confessions from morning to night. He was a man of prayer and suffering. The Pope called the prayer groups the friar had left behind “a great river of people who pray”.

The prayer groups had begun years before. In 1942 Pius XII asked Catholics to pray for peace in the middle of the war. Saint Pio urged the people who came to him to form groups and pray together. A bulletin named after the hospital began to link them in 1949. When he died there were about seven hundred of these prayer groups, with some 68,000 members in fifteen countries. He called them nurseries of faith and hearths of love. The Church approved their statutes in 1986. By 2013 there were about 3,300 groups and some three million members in sixty countries.

The hospital went on too. Saint Pio had held its shares in his own name. In his will he left them to the Holy See, so the Home for the Relief of Suffering became the Pope’s hospital. It still stands beside the friary.

The Church began to study his life six weeks after his death. A first process opened on 4 November 1968, and the formal cause followed in 1982. From 1983 to 1990 a church court at San Giovanni Rotondo gathered the sworn testimony of the people who had known him. In December 1997 the Pope declared that Saint Pio had practised the Christian virtues to a heroic degree. Before the Church could beatify him and call him Blessed, it needed one approved miracle. In November 1995 a woman from Salerno named Consiglia De Martino was in hospital with a ruptured thoracic duct. That is a vessel that carries lymph through the chest. Surgery was set for 3 November. Friar Modestino of Pietrelcina prayed for her at Saint Pio’s tomb. On 3 November the swelling was gone, and she left the hospital without an operation. All five doctors on the Church’s medical board judged the cure scientifically inexplicable, and in December 1998 the Church declared it a miracle.

On 2 May 1999 Pope Saint John Paul II beatified Saint Pio in Saint Peter’s Square, before what one report called the largest crowd ever seen there. The Pope said that by a life given wholly to prayer and to listening to others, this humble Capuchin friar “astonished the world”. He added that he had met the friar himself when he was a student in Rome. One more miracle would make him a saint. It came within the year to the son of one of the doctors in the hospital Saint Pio had built.

Saint John Paul II Canonizes Saint Pio

Matteo Pio Colella was seven years old in January 2000. His father Antonio Colella was a urologist at the Home for the Relief of Suffering, and his mother was Maria Lucia Ippolito. On 20 January the boy came down with a fever, vomiting, and purple spots on his skin. It was bacterial meningitis of the most violent kind. By the next day he was in a coma in his father’s hospital, in septic shock and on a respirator. His heart stopped once and was started again. The doctors told his parents that he would die soon.

His mother went to Saint Pio’s tomb and prayed the Rosary there, with friars beside her. Eight days after he fell ill, Matteo woke up. His mother later told what he said when they asked him what he remembered. He had seen himself asleep on the bed, from far off, and an old man with a white beard and a long brown robe had taken his right hand. “Matteo, don’t worry,” the man had said. “You will get well quickly.” They showed him photographs, and he picked out Saint Pio. A brain scan on 27 January showed no damage. He went home on 6 February.

The Church examined the case with its usual care. A court in the local diocese took evidence from June to October 2000. On 22 November 2001 the medical board of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints found the healing complete, lasting, and scientifically inexplicable. On 20 December 2001 the Church declared it a miracle. The decree of canonization was signed on 26 February 2002.

On 16 June 2002 Saint John Paul II stood in Saint Peter’s Square and declared the friar of Pietrelcina a saint of the Catholic Church. The Pope who did it had gone to the friar for confession as a young man and had sent him a letter in Latin as a bishop. In his sermon he spoke of the confessional.

“I also had the privilege, during my young years, of benefitting from his availability for penitents.”

— Pope Saint John Paul II, homily at the canonization of Saint Pio, 16 June 2002

The Pope went on to say that the ministry of the confessional was one of the marks of Saint Pio’s whole life. It had drawn great crowds to the friary at San Giovanni Rotondo. The Church set his feast on 23 September, the day of his death. One estimate puts the pilgrims at about two million a year. They bring what people always brought him: their sins and their sick. In February 2016 Pope Francis asked for the holy relics of Saint Pio to come to Rome for the Year of Mercy. They were carried in procession down the great avenue to Saint Peter’s with the litany of the saints. The man who had begged God to let him suffer in hiding was honoured in the largest church in the world.

He had said what he was in one line, and the Church put it on his official record. “I want to be only a poor friar who prays.”

A Note on the Sources

Saint Pio’s letters are under copyright. This life quotes them in short lines in our own English from the Italian printed by the Capuchin magazine Voce di Padre Pio. His own letter of 22 October 1918 says he was alone in the choir; the Vatican newspaper’s obituary of 1968 says a friar found him unconscious behind the high altar. We follow the letter. The spoken account to Don Peppino Orlando has no named source or date, so we tell it as a tradition. Cardinal Bertone dates the first marks to 7 September 1910. The first written report is dated 8 September 1911. Italian Wikipedia places the words to Don Pannullo the day after that report, while a news item on a 2022 book says Pannullo learned of the marks in 1910. The boy’s wish to be a friar with a beard survives only in English, and the year of the friar’s visit is given as 1897 and as 1901. The stories that Saint Pio gave himself to Jesus at five and that Padre Agostino found him near death at Venafro each rest on one biography. Sources differ on the coin of 1940. They give 250 or 300 beds for 1956, and 2:20 or 2:30 as the time of death. The two old newspaper pieces are quoted from a 2018 article, and we did not see the originals. The date of the window march of 1923 is not known. No named source gives the line of Pius XI about being badly informed. Writers differ on whether Padre Agostino Gemelli came on his own in 1920 or was sent by Rome. Who ordered the recordings of 1960 is not settled, and one historian says the Vatican did not. English Wikipedia also gives Pope Saint John XXIII a private phrase about Saint Pio, “straw idol”, and we did not find the primary text. The story of the archbishop’s sister and the tapes comes from one Capuchin author and has not been confirmed. Matteo Colella’s words are known from his mother’s account on a devotional website, not from the decree. The historian Sergio Luzzatto published the papers of Saint John XXIII and Maccari in 2007 and added charges of his own. He says that eleven early letters copy long passages from Saint Gemma Galgani and that Saint Pio bought carbolic acid. Saint Pio’s defenders answer that the acid was for sterilizing syringes, and that Bishop Rossi in 1921 saw simplicity and a playful spirit in the man. We have not read Luzzatto’s book or the printed volumes of Saint Pio’s letters.

How This Life Was Researched

Five sets of research notes and fifteen scene cards lie behind this life. They draw on more than fifty sources in Italian, English, Latin, and Spanish. Among them are the official Holy See texts: the address of 1987, the homilies of 1999 and 2002, and the pages of the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints. Cardinal Bertone’s homily of 2008 is another. Others are the Vatican newspaper’s obituary of 1968 and two newspapers of 1920 and 1923. Saint Pio’s letters are quoted with page numbers in Voce di Padre Pio, and the same magazine quotes Padre Agostino’s notebooks. The Capuchin portal prints the diary of Nina Campanile and the memoir of Padre Paolino. Bishop Rossi’s 1921 papers were published in a book in 2008. Padre Pellegrino Funicelli gave an interview about the last night, and John McCaffery wrote an eyewitness book in 1978.

saint.relic_description:
Padre Pio died in his cell at the Capuchin friary of San Giovanni Rotondo at about 2:30 a.m. on 23 September 1968, and about 100,000 people came to his funeral on 26 September. He was buried at San Giovanni Rotondo. His stigmata had faded before his death, and the doctor who examined his body is said to have found no wounds and no scars.

The tomb was opened after midnight on 3 March 2008. Archbishop D’Ambrosio reported the body in fair condition: the skull partly skeletal, the chin and body well preserved, the hands looking as if manicured, and no visible stigmata. A silicone mask modeled on a 1968 photograph was made for the display. The body was shown from 24 April 2008, when Cardinal Saraiva Martins celebrated Mass for about 15,000 people, and the display was extended to September 2009. In April 2010 the remains were moved to a new crypt decorated in gold in the sanctuary at San Giovanni Rotondo.

In February 2016, at the request of Pope Francis, his relics and those of St. Leopold Mandic were carried in procession down the Via della Conciliazione into St. Peter’s Basilica for the Jubilee of Mercy, and were there on Ash Wednesday, 10 February. Aleteia gives 5 to 11 February; another source gives 8 to 14 February. No miracle was claimed for the condition of the body, and the archbishop’s report did not call it incorrupt.
